claim: SARS-CoV-2 is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the viral causative agent of COVID-19, is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population, killing a confirmed ~ 5 million but likely considerably more.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the estimated infection rate of SARS-CoV-2 presented in the introduction.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 has killed a confirmed ~5 million people but likely considerably more.
source: SARS-CoV-2, the viral causative agent of COVID-19, is estimated to have infected some 10% of the world's population, killing a confirmed ~ 5 million but likely considerably more.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the death toll from COVID-19 presented in the introduction.

claim: Inequities in vaccine distribution, waning immunity, biological and behavioral diversity of the human population, and emergence of viral variants challenge current and future containment of COVID-19.
source: Despite the great promise of vaccines, the pandemic is ongoing; inequities in vaccine distribution, waning immunity, the biological and behavioral diversity of the human population, the emergence of viral variants that compromise monoclonal therapies and vaccine efficacy, all challenge current and future containment (Diamond et al., 2021; Lavine et al., 2021; Fraser et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2021a; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Spike (S) is the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion.
source: Spike (S), the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion, is key for infection as it attaches the virion to its cognate host surface receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein, and triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Spike attaches the virion to ACE2 and triggers fusion between host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm.
source: Spike (S), the major surface envelope glycoprotein of the SARS-CoV-2 virion, is key for infection as it attaches the virion to its cognate host surface receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) protein, and triggers fusion between the host and viral membranes, leading to viral entry into the cytoplasm (Zhou et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020b; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation.
source: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation, and exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the molecular weight of the spike protein.

claim: Spike exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
source: The spike protein monomer is ~140 kDa, or ~180–200 kDa including its extensive glycosylation, and exists as a homotrimer on the viral surface.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the oligomeric state of spike on the viral surface.

claim: Spike is composed of two domains: S1, which contains the host receptor binding domain (RBD); and S2, which undergoes large conformational changes that enable fusion of the viral membrane with that of its host.
source: Spike is highly dynamic and is composed of two domains: S1, which contains the host receptor binding domain (RBD); and S2, which undergoes large conformational changes that enable fusion of the viral membrane with that of its host (Li et al., 2003; Li, 2016; Letko et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020; Hsieh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The major target of immunotherapeutics has been the RBD.
source: Based on its requirement for entry, the major target of immunotherapeutics has been the RBD (Hartenian et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Baum et al., 2020; Finkelstein et al., 2021; Korber et al., 2020; Trigueiro-Louro et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Current therapies face the emergence of variants, particularly RBD point mutants, which have evolved to bypass the most potent neutralizing human antibodies.
source: Major immunotherapeutic strategies to date have focused on immune sera and human monoclonal antibodies; however, these therapies now face the emergence of variants, particularly RBD point mutants, which have evolved to bypass the most potent neutralizing human antibodies (Wang et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2021a; Weisblum et al., 2020; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Starr et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Nanobodies are the smallest single-domain antigen binding proteins identified to date.
source: Nanobodies are the smallest single-domain antigen binding proteins identified to date, possessing several potential advantages over conventional monoclonal antibodies.
evidence: This is a factual statement about nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of variant heavy chain-only IgGs (HCAb) found in camelids.
source: Nanobodies are derived from the variable domain (VHH) of variant heavy chain-only IgGs (HCAb) found in camelids (e.g., llamas, alpacas, and camels).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the origin of nanobodies.

claim: Nanobodies can bind in modes different from typical antibodies, covering more chemical space and binding with very high affinities.
source: They can bind in modes different from typical antibodies, covering more chemical space and binding with very high affinities (comparable to the very best antibodies) (Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020; Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The small size of nanobodies (~15 kDa) allows them to bind tightly to otherwise inaccessible epitopes.
source: Their small size (~15 kDa) allows them to bind tightly to otherwise inaccessible epitopes that may be obscured by the glycoprotein coat, as well as minimizing issues of steric hindrance of multiple antibodies binding to adjacent epitopes as observed with larger immunoglobulin G molecules (Corti et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Nanobodies are highly soluble, very stable, lack glycans, and are readily cloned and produced in bacteria or yeast.
source: Nanobodies are also highly soluble, very stable, lack glycans, and are readily cloned and produced in bacteria or yeast (Muyldermans, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Nanobodies have low immunogenicity.
source: They have low immunogenicity (Revets et al., 2005; Jovčevska and Muyldermans, 2020; Bannas et al., 2017) and can be readily 'humanized' (including Fc addition), modified to alter clearance rates, derivatized, combined for synergistic activity, and multimerized to improve characteristics (Chanier and Chames, 2019; Vincke et al., 2009; Duggan, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A major advantage of nanobodies is their potential for direct delivery by nebulization deep into the lungs.
source: In the case of respiratory viruses like SARS-CoV-2, nanobodies' flexibility in drug delivery is a critical advantage. Beyond typical administration methods, a major advantage of nanobodies is their potential for direct delivery by nebulization deep into the lungs (Wölfel et al., 2020; Nambulli et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Direct delivery by nebulization can provide a high local concentration in the airways and lungs to ensure rapid onset of therapeutic effects, while limiting the potential for unwanted systemic effects.
source: This route can provide a high local concentration in the airways and lungs to ensure rapid onset of therapeutic effects, while limiting the potential for unwanted systemic effects (Erreni et al., 2020) as exemplified by clinical trials (Van Heeke et al., 2017; Zare et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Nanobodies are relatively inexpensive and easy to reproducibly manufacture, with long shelf-lives and greater inherent stability compared to other biologicals.
source: Moreover, with respect to deployment, nanobodies are relatively inexpensive and easy to reproducibly manufacture, with long shelf-lives and greater inherent stability compared to other biologicals, including monoclonals.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the manufacturing and stability properties of nanobodies.

claim: There are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: To date, there are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike and those that are available primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation (Niu et al., 2021; Raybould et al., 2021; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2020a; Pymm et al., 2021; Hanke et al., 2020; Custódio et al., 2020; Esparza et al., 2020; Wrapp, 2020a; Dong et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Available nanobodies primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation.
source: To date, there are 453 nanobodies available against SARS-CoV-2 spike and those that are available primarily recognize regions of RBD with many subject to escape variation (Niu et al., 2021; Raybould et al., 2021; Schoof et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020; Koenig et al., 2021; Huo et al., 2020a; Pymm et al., 2021; Hanke et al., 2020; Custódio et al., 2020; Esparza et al., 2020; Wrapp, 2020a; Dong et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The authors generated a large repertoire of nanobodies to saturate the distinct and highly conserved available epitope space of SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: We therefore generated a large nanobody repertoire to saturate the distinct and highly conserved available epitope space of SARS-CoV-2 spike, including the S1 receptor binding domain, N-terminal domain, and the S2 subunit, to identify new nanobody binding sites that may reflect novel mechanisms of viral neutralization.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objective and approach.

claim: The generated nanobodies are highly stable monovalent nanobodies that potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Structural mapping and functional assays show that indeed these highly stable monovalent nanobodies potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection, display numerous neutralization mechanisms, are effective against emerging variants of concern, and are resistant to mutational escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural mapping and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: The generated nanobodies display numerous neutralization mechanisms.
source: Structural mapping and functional assays show that indeed these highly stable monovalent nanobodies potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection, display numerous neutralization mechanisms, are effective against emerging variants of concern, and are resistant to mutational escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural mapping and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: The generated nanobodies are effective against emerging variants of concern.
source: Structural mapping and functional assays show that indeed these highly stable monovalent nanobodies potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection, display numerous neutralization mechanisms, are effective against emerging variants of concern, and are resistant to mutational escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural mapping and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: The generated nanobodies are resistant to mutational escape.
source: Structural mapping and functional assays show that indeed these highly stable monovalent nanobodies potently inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection, display numerous neutralization mechanisms, are effective against emerging variants of concern, and are resistant to mutational escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural mapping and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Rational combinations of these nanobodies that bind to distinct sites within and between spike subunits exhibit extraordinary synergy.
source: Rational combinations of these nanobodies that bind to distinct sites within and between spike subunits exhibit extraordinary synergy and suggest multiple tailored therapeutic and prophylactic strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: 374 high-confidence CDR3 sequences were identified from the mass spectrometry workflow.
source: A network visualization of 374 high-confidence CDR3 sequences identified from the mass spectrometry workflow.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1B and the text describing the mass spectrometry workflow.

claim: The 374 CDR3 sequences formed 183 isolated components when connected by edges defined by a Damerau–Levenshtein distance of no more than 3.
source: Nodes (CDR3 sequences) were connected by edges defined by a Damerau–Levenshtein distance of no more than 3, forming 183 isolated components.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1B and the text describing the network analysis.

claim: 116 nanobodies were selected for further characterization.
source: This filtering identified the top 116 nanobodies that were purified for further characterization (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a statement of the number of nanobodies selected for further study.

claim: All 116 selected nanobodies bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM.
source: All bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM, and two with single-digit picomolar affinities (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Two nanobodies bound with single-digit picomolar affinities.
source: All bound with high affinity, with >60% binding with KDs < 1 nM, and two with single-digit picomolar affinities (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: 71 nanobodies targeted RBD, 19 targeted non-RBD regions of S1, and 26 bind S2.
source: While most S1-binding nanobodies bind RBD (71 nanobodies), 19 targeted non-RBD regions of S1 and 26 bind S2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the binding data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The lower number of non-RBD S1 and S2 nanobodies likely reflects the highly antigenic nature of the RBD and the occlusion of non-RBD S1 regions and S2 due to the glycan shield of SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: The lower number of non-RBD S1 and S2 nanobodies likely reflects the highly antigenic nature of the RBD and the occlusion of non-RBD S1 regions and S2 due to the glycan shield of SARS-CoV-2 spike (Grant et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Many nanobodies have fast association rates (kon ≥ 10+6).
source: While both high on rates and low off rates contributed to these high affinities, kinetic analyses underscore the generally fast association rates (many with kon ≥ 10+6) of these nanobodies (likely due to their small size and proportionally large paratope surface area), with many surpassing the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5) (Tian et al., 2020; Figure 2), a property that would benefit translation of these nanobodies into rapid therapeutics and diagnostics (Carter, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Many nanobodies surpass the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5).
source: While both high on rates and low off rates contributed to these high affinities, kinetic analyses underscore the generally fast association rates (many with kon ≥ 10+6) of these nanobodies (likely due to their small size and proportionally large paratope surface area), with many surpassing the kon of high-performing monoclonal antibodies (kon ~ 10+5) (Tian et al., 2020; Figure 2), a property that would benefit translation of these nanobodies into rapid therapeutics and diagnostics (Carter, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2, and a citation to a published study.

claim: Six out of seven tested nanobodies retained very strong binding to both B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha and B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta variants.
source: Of the seven nanobodies tested, six of these (S1-1, S1-6, S1-RBD-9, S1-RBD-11, S1-RBD-15, and S1-RBD-35) retained their very strong binding to both variants, with only a modest reduction in affinity for S1-RBD-11 binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta (20–161 pM).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Table 3.

claim: S1-23 binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was reduced from a KD of 17 pM to 230 pM.
source: For the seventh nanobody, S1-23, binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was only reduced from a KD of 17 pM to a still-respectable 230 pM, although its binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Table 3.

claim: S1-23 binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished.
source: For the seventh nanobody, S1-23, binding to variant B.1.1.7/20I/501Y.V1/alpha was only reduced from a KD of 17 pM to a still-respectable 230 pM, although its binding to variant B.1.351/20H/501Y.V2/beta was abolished (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR data presented in Figure 2 and Table 3.

claim: All but two nanobodies fall within a Tm range between 50 and 80°C.
source: Each nanobody plotted against their Tm as measured by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), revealing all but two nanobodies fall within a Tm range between 50 and 80°C, where the bulk of our nanobodies have a Tm ≥ 60°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by the DSF data presented in Figure 2D and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The bulk of the nanobodies have a Tm ≥ 60°C.
source: Each nanobody plotted against their Tm as measured by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), revealing all but two nanobodies fall within a Tm range between 50 and 80°C, where the bulk of our nanobodies have a Tm ≥ 60°C.
evidence: This claim is supported by the DSF data presented in Figure 2D and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Freeze-drying without cryoprotectants did not significantly affect nanobody stability, kinetics, and affinity.
source: The results revealed no significant effect on stability, kinetics, and affinity (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SPR and DSF data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Epitope binning revealed three large, mostly non-overlapping bins for RBD-binding nanobodies.
source: This approach revealed three large, mostly non-overlapping bins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the epitope binning data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Each RBD bin contained smaller, better-correlated clusters of nanobodies, indicating the presence of numerous distinct sub-epitope bins.
source: However, each bin contained smaller, better-correlated clusters of nanobodies, reflected by the dendrogram, indicating the presence of numerous distinct sub-epitope bins present within each larger bin, that is, discrete epitopes that partially overlap with other discrete epitopes in the same bin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the epitope binning data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: At least eight epitope bins were discerned for RBD-binding nanobodies using the gap statistic.
source: We calculated the gap statistic (Tibshirani et al., 2001), to estimate the optimal cluster number, discerning at least eight epitope bins (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the epitope binning data presented in Figure 3A and the gap statistic calculation.

claim: As many as four S1-non-RBD bins and five S2 bins were revealed by epitope binning.
source: Pearson's correlation coefficients were used to hierarchically cluster these nanobodies, revealing as many as four S1-non-RBD bins and five S2 bins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the epitope binning data presented in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mass photometry demonstrated that at least three different nanobodies can bind simultaneously to the RBD.
source: These data confirmed the separation of our major epitope bins, and furthermore demonstrated that we can bind at least three different nanobodies simultaneously to the RBD, contrasting with the much larger conventional immunoglobulins, which may be too large to simultaneously bind either monomer or trimer S protein (Corti et al., 2021; Stewart et al., 1997; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass photometry data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: 36% of the monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: 23% of the monomeric nanobody repertoire showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: 17 nanobodies are potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower.
source: Overall, 36% of our monomeric nanobody repertoire neutralized with IC50s ≤ 100 nM, while 23% showed neutralization with IC50s < 50 nM and 17 potent neutralizers at 20 nM or lower (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The most potent neutralizing nanobodies mapped to the RBD.
source: Our most potent neutralizing nanobodies mapped to the RBD; neutralizing activity mapped to each of the major epitope bins of the RBD and were of similar efficacy to the most potent of the comparison nanobodies; importantly, nanobodies binding outside of the RBD also possess neutralizing activity (for example S1-64 and S1-65).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Nanobodies binding outside of the RBD also possess neutralizing activity.
source: Our most potent neutralizing nanobodies mapped to the RBD; neutralizing activity mapped to each of the major epitope bins of the RBD and were of similar efficacy to the most potent of the comparison nanobodies; importantly, nanobodies binding outside of the RBD also possess neutralizing activity (for example S1-64 and S1-65).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Nanobodies mapping outside of the RBD on S1 (anti-S1, non-RBD) and to S2 neutralized the pseudovirus, albeit with somewhat higher IC50s.
source: Notably, nanobodies mapping outside of the RBD on S1 (anti-S1, non-RBD) and to S2 also neutralized the pseudovirus in our assay, albeit with somewhat higher IC50s (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4B and C.

claim: This is the first evidence of nanobody neutralization activity mapping outside of the RBD.
source: This is the first evidence of nanobody neutralization activity mapping outside of the RBD.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Oligomerization of most nanobodies significantly improved their IC50s and measured affinities.
source: Oligomerization of most of our nanobodies significantly improved their IC50s and measured affinities (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the oligomerization data presented in Table 4.

claim: Dimerization and trimerization of S1-RBD-35 improved neutralization activity from IC50s of ~12 nM to ~150 pM and ~70 pM, respectively.
source: For example, dimerization and trimerization of S1-RBD-35 improved neutralization activity from IC50s of ~12 nM to ~150 pM and ~70 pM, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the oligomerization data presented in Table 4.

claim: Dimerization and trimerization of S1-23 improved neutralization from ~6 nM to ~220 pM and ~90 pM, respectively.
source: Similar results were found with S1-23, improving neutralization from ~6 nM to ~220 pM and ~90 pM, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the oligomerization data presented in Figure 4D and Table 4.

claim: Dimerization of S2-7 converted a non-neutralizing nanobody to one having a respectable neutralizing activity (IC50 ~ 250 nM).
source: This includes S2-7, for which dimerization converted a nanobody that we considered to be a non-neutralizer to one having a respectable neutralizing activity (IC50 ~ 250 nM), with further potency achieved by trimerization and tetramerization, down to an IC50 of ~30 nM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the oligomerization data presented in Figure 4F and Table 4.

claim: All nanobodies tested neutralized the alpha variant.
source: While all nanobodies neutralize the alpha variant, S1-23 showed an almost 14-fold drop in potency (Figure 4A and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: S1-23 showed an almost 14-fold drop in potency against the alpha variant.
source: While all nanobodies neutralize the alpha variant, S1-23 showed an almost 14-fold drop in potency (Figure 4A and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: S1-23 and S1-62 failed to neutralize the beta and gamma variants.
source: S1-23 and S1-62 failed to neutralize the beta and gamma variants, while S1-1 and S1-RBD-15 were as efficacious against all three VOCs as they were against wild-type spike (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4I and J.

claim: S1-1 and S1-RBD-15 were as efficacious against all three VOCs as they were against wild-type spike.
source: S1-23 and S1-62 failed to neutralize the beta and gamma variants, while S1-1 and S1-RBD-15 were as efficacious against all three VOCs as they were against wild-type spike (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4I and J.

claim: S1-RBD-9 showed increased neutralization activity against all three VOC, improving ~2-fold against alpha, ~6-fold against beta, and ~10-fold against gamma.
source: Remarkably, S1-RBD-9 showed increased neutralization activity against all three VOC, improving ~2-fold against alpha, ~6-fold against beta, and ~10-fold against gamma (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Seven out of 27 anti-RBD monomer nanobodies tested displayed excellent neutralizing activities against SARS-CoV-1 spike pseudotyped virus.
source: Of the nanobodies tested in this assay, several (7 of 27 tested) of our anti-RBD monomer nanobodies also displayed excellent neutralizing activities against SARS-CoV-1 spike pseudotyped virus (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4K.

claim: S1-1, S1-39 and S1-RBD-6 had similar IC50s against both SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV-1 pseudotypes.
source: S1-1, S1-39 and S1-RBD-6 had similar IC50s against both pseudotypes, while S1-35 and S1-6 showed reduced activity against SARS-CoV-1 pseudotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4K and Table 5.

claim: S1-23, S1-37, and S1-48 showed no activity against SARS-CoV-1 spike pseudotypes.
source: Notably, S1-23, S1-37, and S1-48 showed no activity against SARS-CoV-1 spike pseudotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the pseudovirus neutralization data presented in Figure 4K and Table 5.

claim: All nanobodies tested that neutralized pseudovirus also showed potent neutralization by plaque and focus reduction assays with authentic SARS-CoV-2.
source: All nanobodies tested that neutralized pseudovirus also showed potent neutralization by plaque and focus reduction assays and correlated well with our pseudovirus assays (Figure 5A, Table 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authentic virus neutralization data presented in Figure 5A and Table 6.

claim: S1-1 potently neutralized SARS-CoV-2 at each concentration tested in primary human airway epithelial cells.
source: S1-1 potently neutralized SARS-CoV-2 at each concentration tested while S1-23 inhibited SARS-CoV-2 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the primary airway epithelial cell data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: S1-23 inhibited SARS-CoV-2 in a dose-dependent manner in primary human airway epithelial cells.
source: S1-1 potently neutralized SARS-CoV-2 at each concentration tested while S1-23 inhibited SARS-CoV-2 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the primary airway epithelial cell data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The efficacy of the S1-23 nanobody was strongly enhanced when provided to cells as a trimer.
source: The efficacy of the S1-23 nanobody was strongly enhanced when provided to cells as a trimer, potently inhibiting viral replication (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the primary airway epithelial cell data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: 32 unique rVSV-SARs-CoV-2/GFP mutants that exhibited resistance to one or more of 22 representative neutralizing nanobodies were identified.
source: We thus identified 32 unique rVSV-SARs-CoV-2/GFP mutants that exhibited resistance to one or more of 22 representative neutralizing nanobodies against diverse spike epitopes (Table 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data presented in Table 7.

claim: Some of the most potently neutralizing nanobodies selected resistant mutations at the same positions (e.g., E484K) as those selected by potent neutralizing antibodies cloned from SARS-CoV-2 convalescents and vaccine recipients.
source: Some of the most potently neutralizing nanobodies selected resistant mutations at the same positions (e.g., E484K) as those selected by potent neutralizing antibodies that have been cloned from SARS-CoV-2 convalescents and vaccine recipients, confirming that the ACE2 binding site is a point of particular vulnerability for potent neutralization.
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data presented in Table 7 and comparison to published antibody data.

claim: Other nanobodies selected mutations that have not previously been encountered in human antibody selection experiments.
source: Additionally, however, other nanobodies selected mutations that have not previously been encountered in human antibody selection experiments (Table 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data presented in Table 7.

claim: When nanobodies were combined in cocktails containing two nanobodies, in eight out of nine cases, no infectious rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was recovered after two passages.
source: In contrast, when nanobodies were combined in cocktails containing two nanobodies, at the same total concentration as was used for the individual nanobodies, in eight out of nine cases, no infectious rVSV/SARS-CoV-2/GFP was recovered after two passages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Combining two nanobodies imposed the requirement for a minimum of two amino acid substitutions to confer resistance to the nanobody cocktail.
source: These results show that simply combining two nanobodies imposed the requirement for a minimum of two amino acid substitutions to confer resistance to the nanobody cocktail, greatly elevating the genetic barrier for escape.
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Integrative structural models were generated for 21 different neutralizing nanobodies.
source: In sum, we solved integrative structures for 21 different neutralizing nanobodies that, based on our epitope binning data, appeared to collectively explore much of the spike surface, with 18 recognizing RBD, 1 recognizing the NTD of S1, and 2 recognizing S2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The 21 nanobodies are classified into 10 groups based on overlapping footprints.
source: Based on overlapping footprints, these 21 nanobodies are classified into 10 groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Neutralizing nanobodies bind at sites that are complementary to sites of glycosylation.
source: As expected, neutralizing nanobodies bind at sites that are complementary to sites of glycosylation, which entropically shield larger zones than represented (Casalino et al., 2020), and are instead concentrated at the largely glycan-free RBD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6 and a citation to a published study.

claim: ~80% of anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing.
source: Indeed, among our entire repertoire, epitope binning shows that neutralization activity, corresponding escape mutants, and the mapped epitopes are heavily concentrated on the RBD (Figures 3, 4 and 6); ~80% of our anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing, with many escape mutants mapping adjacent to the receptor-binding motif (RBM), the region of RBD that interacts directly with ACE2 and is most lightly glycosylated (Shajahan et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020), whereas ~20% of our anti-S2 nanobodies and ~60% of our non-RBD anti-S1 nanobodies are neutralizing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neutralization data presented in Figures 3, 4, and 6.

claim: ~20% of anti-S2 nanobodies are neutralizing.
source: Indeed, among our entire repertoire, epitope binning shows that neutralization activity, corresponding escape mutants, and the mapped epitopes are heavily concentrated on the RBD (Figures 3, 4 and 6); ~80% of our anti-RBD nanobodies are neutralizing, with many escape mutants mapping adjacent to the receptor-binding motif (RBM), the region of RBD that interacts directly with ACE2 and is most lightly glycosylated (Shajahan et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020), whereas ~20% of our anti-S2 nanobodies and ~60% of our non-RBD anti-S1 nanobodies are neutralizing.

claim: The RBD-binding nanobodies fall into at least seven groups.
source: Our RBD-binding nanobodies fall into at least seven groups (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Many mapped nanobodies bind epitopes that partially overlap with previously defined classes of IgG-binding epitopes, but are more compact due to the smaller nanobody paratopes.
source: Many of our mapped nanobodies bind epitopes that partially overlap with previously defined classes of IgG-binding epitopes, but are more compact due to the smaller nanobody paratopes (Corti et al., 2021; Barnes et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021); however, many others define previously unreported binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6 and citations to published studies.

claim: Many nanobodies define previously unreported binding sites.
source: Many of our mapped nanobodies bind epitopes that partially overlap with previously defined classes of IgG-binding epitopes, but are more compact due to the smaller nanobody paratopes (Corti et al., 2021; Barnes et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021); however, many others define previously unreported binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: S1-49 binds to the NTD of spike.
source: S1-49, which is a member of group 8 (Figure 6), binds to the NTD for which neutralization activities remain unclear (McCallum et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: S2-10 and S2-40 are the first neutralizing nanobodies that bind to S2.
source: Here, we present the first neutralizing nanobodies that bind to S2 (groups 9 and 10) (Figures 2, 4 and 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling and neutralization data presented in Figures 2, 4, and 6.

claim: The S2-10 escape mutant S982R indicates binding at S982 of spike, positioned at the end of the highly conserved heptad repeat 1.
source: For example, the S2-10 escape mutant S982R (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates binding at S982 of spike, positioned at the end of the highly conserved heptad repeat 1, within a region of the S2 that undergoes large dynamic changes as the protein adopts a post fusion conformation; this suggests that S2-10 may restrict this conformational change, thereby inhibiting viral fusion (Cai et al., 2020; Pierri, 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the escape mutant data and integrative modeling presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: S2-10 may restrict the conformational change of S2, thereby inhibiting viral fusion.
source: For example, the S2-10 escape mutant S982R (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) indicates binding at S982 of spike, positioned at the end of the highly conserved heptad repeat 1, within a region of the S2 that undergoes large dynamic changes as the protein adopts a post fusion conformation; this suggests that S2-10 may restrict this conformational change, thereby inhibiting viral fusion (Cai et al., 2020; Pierri, 2020; Turoňová et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the escape mutant data and integrative modeling, supported by citations to published studies.

claim: S2-40 sits at the interface between spike subunits.
source: S2-40 uniquely sits at the interface between spike subunits, which raises fascinating possibilities for its neutralizing activity, perhaps involving the alteration of spike's quaternary structure or dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integrative modeling data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Powerfully synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs.
source: Indeed, powerfully synergistic effects were observed between numerous nanobody pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The combination of S1-23 and S1-1 dramatically increased the potency of both nanobodies by ~32- and ~ 21-fold, respectively.
source: For example, the combination of S1-23 and S1-1, which bind to opposite sides of the RBD, dramatically increased the potency of both nanobodies by ~32- and ~ 21-fold, respectively (Figure 7B, Table 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7B and Table 9.

claim: S1-RBD-15 had a greater influence on S1-23, promoting its potency by ~300-fold.
source: S1-RBD-15, which binds to a similar epitope as S1-1, shows corresponding synergy with S1-23, suggesting that synergy may be predictable based on epitope mapping (Figure 7C). In this case, however, S1-RBD-15 had a greater influence on S1-23, promoting its potency by ~300-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7C and Table 9.

claim: S1-49 substantially improved the neutralization potency of either S1-1 or S1-RBD-15.
source: S1-49, which binds to the NTD of spike (Figure 6), substantially improved the neutralization potency of either S1-1 or S1-RBD-15 (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7G and H.

claim: The synergy observed with S1-49 with S1-1 elicited a >1000-fold increase in potency.
source: The synergy observed with S1-49 with S1-1 elicited a >1000-fold increase in potency.
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7G and Table 9.

claim: The synergy was greatest with the S2-10-dimer, which showed >4000-fold increase in potency when combined with either S1-23 or S1-RBD-15.
source: Interestingly, among all the nanobody pairs that we tested, the synergy was greatest with the S2-10-dimer, which showed >4000-fold increase in potency when combined with either S1-23 or S1-RBD-15 (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by the synergy data presented in Figure 7I and J and Table 9.
